proof:
# Sharp active-normal rank bound via a centered Ball radial body

Let K be a full-dimensional compact convex body in R^d, let y_* be an
ACTUAL point of maximum ordinary halfspace depth, and write

    A(K)=min_(u!=0) |K intersect {u.(x-y_*)>=0}|,
    D(K)=A(K)/|K|,       Gamma_s=(s/(s+1))^s.

Thus A is UNNORMALIZED cap mass and D is normalized maximum depth.

**Theorem.** Suppose a finite family of actual minimizing cap normals
u_i at y_* has a positive balance sum_i lambda_i u_i=0 and spans a
space of dimension r. Then

    D(K)>=Gamma_r.                                          (1)

In particular, if ALL minimizing normals span a proper subspace of
rank r<d, the same bound holds. For every 2<=r<d, (1) is sharp even
when the complete active-normal set spans exactly r dimensions.
Rank one cannot be the complete active-normal span when d>1.

The argument uses a genuine projected uniform density and an existential
radial centering theorem. It does not replace an arbitrary marked point
by its centroid, invoke a secondary-objective KKT condition, or infer
anything about an arbitrary partial list of critical normals lacking
positive balance.

## 1. The exact ordinary background input

We use Ball's non-even radial-body theorem in the precise form stated
and proved as Theorem 2.2 in B. Klartag,
[On convex perturbations with a bounded isotropic constant](https://www.math.tau.ac.il/~klartagb/papers/perturb.pdf),
p. 5 of the PDF (local copy: `background-radial-body/klartag-convex-perturbations-bounded-isotropic.pdf`): if f:R^r->[0,infinity) is log-concave, f(0)>0,
and p>=1, then

    K_p(f)={v: integral_0^infinity f(tv)t^(p-1)dt>=f(0)/p}

is convex. Klartag explicitly supplies the non-even adaptation.
Neither evenness nor attainment of the maximum at the origin is a
hypothesis. We use only p=r, a positive integer, and bounded compactly
supported f positive in the interior of its full-dimensional support.
No unbounded-density or unbounded-support extension is asserted here.

The other ordinary inputs are Brouwer's fixed-point theorem, Euclidean
projection onto a compact convex set, ordinary Brunn--Minkowski, and the
ordinary centroid Gruenbaum inequality in dimension r. The sharpness
example additionally uses the already proved paired-tail theorem in
`candidate 732b11a769399016`.

### Self-contained archived proof and the stronger inverse-power corollary

The external radial-convexity input can instead be supplied by the fully
self-contained theorem in
`candidate 1c081cc96e28cc4a`.
I audited its complete quantile/Holder proof: PASS. In its notation,
t=a r_1+b r_2 follows exactly from a=lambda t/r_1 and
b=(1-lambda)t/r_2; differentiation gives
 t'=t[aX^beta/r_1^r+bY^beta/r_2^r]. Weighted Holder contributes
[a r_1^(r/(beta-1))+b r_2^(r/(beta-1))]^(beta-1)<=t^r,
with the required direction and the exact threshold beta>=r+1.
Together these imply its integrand lower bound one. Integrability rules
out zero inverse density, supplies the needed global radial majorant,
and the quantile changes of variables preserve the full ray integrals.
No correction to that archived proof is needed.

For log-concave f, the extended function f^(-1/beta) is convex for any
beta>0: it is exp((-log f)/beta) on the positive support, with infinity
elsewhere. Thus beta=r+1 invokes the archived theorem and makes the
present radial-convexity step self-contained within the workspace.

Moreover the proof in Section 2 uses log-concavity ONLY to obtain convex
radial bodies and continuity inside the support. It therefore proves the
stronger compact-support corollary: if a bounded density f is positive
on the interior of a compact full-dimensional convex support and its
extended inverse power f^(-1/beta) is convex for some beta>=r+1, then
there exists a point of halfspace mass depth at least Gamma_r integral f.
The finite inverse power is continuous in the interior, so all the
continuity hypotheses used below follow. No unbounded-support extension
is asserted. Positive affine inverse-power densities on compact convex
supports are concrete additional examples covered by this corollary.

## 2. A bounded compact log-concave density admits a Gamma_r center

Let D subset R^r be a compact convex body and f a bounded log-concave
density, positive and continuous on int D and zero outside D. Values on
partial D may be set to zero: this preserves log-concavity and every
integral below. Set W=integral f>0. We prove that there exists x_* in
int D with

    integral_H f >= Gamma_r W
    for every closed halfspace H containing x_*.            (2)

For x in D and u on the unit sphere S^(r-1), define

    a_x(u)=r integral_0^infinity t^(r-1) f(x+tu)dt,
    rho_x(u)=a_x(u)^(1/r),
    L_x={tu: u in S^(r-1), 0<=t<=rho_x(u)}.                 (3)

We include the origin in L_x. Use ordinary spherical measure, with
counting measure on S^0={-1,+1} when r=1. Polar integration gives

    |L_x|=(1/r) integral_S a_x(u)d sigma(u)=W,              (4)
    m(x)=(1/[(r+1)W]) integral_S u a_x(u)^((r+1)/r)d sigma. (5)

Thus m(x) is the centroid vector of this radial set, even at boundary
x where convexity is not needed. Its volume denominator is EXACTLY
constant, independently of x.

For interior x, f(x)>0 and

    L_x=f(x)^(1/r) K_r(v -> f(x+v)).                        (6)

The primary theorem in Section 1 makes L_x convex. It is a genuine
compact full-dimensional body: an interior ball at x gives strictly
positive radial lower bounds, boundedness of f and diam(D) gives a
finite upper bound, and the radial integrals are continuous in u.
For the last assertion, a ray from an interior x meets partial D in
at most its terminal point; dominated convergence applies as u varies.

Crucially, for every u_0!=0, polar integration also gives

    |L_x intersect {v:u_0.v>=0}|
       =integral_{y:u_0.(y-x)>=0} f(y)dy.                  (7)

No Jacobian depending on the cap direction occurs. The construction
preserves all through-x halfspace masses simultaneously.

### Continuity of the centroid vector up to the boundary

Write R=diam(D) and B=sup f. For every x in D and every u, the integral
in (3) is supported on 0<=t<=R and 0<=a_x(u)<=B R^r.
If x_j->x, then f(x_j+tu)->f(x+tu) whenever x+tu is off partial D:
f is continuous in int D and identically zero in the open exterior.
The exceptional set has product spherical-times-dt measure zero. Indeed
partial D has r-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero, so polar integration
about the FIXED x gives the assertion on each interval t>=1/l; take
the countable union over l. This also covers boundary origins and r=1.

Fubini and dominated convergence consequently give a_xj(u)->a_x(u)
for almost every u. The uniform bound B R^r and formula (5) then prove
m(x_j)->m(x). Hence m is continuous on all compact D.

### Strict inward direction at each boundary point

Let x belong to partial D, and let v!=0 be any outward support normal,
so v.(y-x)<=0 for all y in D. If v.u>=0, the ray x+tu is either outside
D or stays in its supporting hyperplane, where we assigned f=0.
Thus a_x(u)=0 for such directions. On an open cone of directions into
an interior ball of D, however, a_x(u)>0 and v.u<0. Formula (5) yields

    v.m(x)<0                                                (8)

for EVERY nonzero outward support normal at x. This is a strict sign,
not a non-strict normal-cone assertion.

### The fixed point and its actual centroid

The continuous map

    F(x)=proj_D(x+m(x))

maps compact convex D to itself. Brouwer gives x_*=F(x_*).
The projection characterization says m(x_*) belongs to the outward
normal cone N_D(x_*). A boundary fixed point is impossible: if m=0,
(8) fails for any nonzero outward support normal; if m!=0, use v=m
in (8) to obtain |m|^2<0. Therefore x_* belongs to int D. Projection
at an interior fixed point implies m(x_*)=0.

By (6), L_x* is an ordinary r-dimensional convex body whose actual
centroid is the origin. Ordinary Gruenbaum and (4), (7) prove (2) for
halfspaces with boundary through x_*. Every containing halfspace contains
its parallel through-point halfspace, so (2) follows for all containing
closed halfspaces. This completes the radial centering proof.

The center x_* is generally not the mean of f. For the exact scalar
calibration f(t)=2t on [0,1], a_x(+)=1-x^2 and a_x(-)=x^2. Hence
L_x=[-x^2,1-x^2], m(x)=(1-2x^2)/2, and x_*=1/sqrt(2), the median;
the mean is 2/3. This checks both the normalization and the center choice.

## 3. A balanced critical circuit fixes the projected maximum exactly

Let U=span{u_i}, dim U=r, and let pi_U be orthogonal projection.
Push forward ordinary volume of K to U. Its density is

    f(z)=H_(d-r)(K intersect (z+U-perp)),                  (9)

with the usual constant-density interpretation when r=d. The density
is bounded, its support D=pi_U(K) is a compact r-dimensional convex
body, and it is positive and continuous on int D. Brunn--Minkowski
makes f^(1/(d-r)) concave when r<d; in particular f is log-concave.
Its integral is |K|. Boundary values do not affect the pushforward law.
These are exactly the hypotheses established in Section 2, not an
appeal to arbitrary log-concave probability lore.

Put p=pi_U(y_*), and let nu=f dz. Every halfspace in U through p lifts
to an ambient halfspace through y_*. Its nu-mass is therefore at least
A(K). Each selected active normal belongs to U and gives equality.
Consequently the projected depth of p is exactly A(K).

In fact its projected MAXIMUM depth is exactly A(K). Given any z in U,
positive balance gives at least one index i with

    u_i.(z-p)>=0.

The halfspace {w:u_i.w>=u_i.z} contains z and is contained in the
critical halfspace {w:u_i.w>=u_i.p}; its nu-mass is at most A(K).
Thus no point z has greater projected depth. Applying (2) to the
actual projected density proves

    A(K)=max depth_nu >= Gamma_r |K|,

which is (1). No assumption that the original ordinary centroid equals
y_* was used, and no claim that the radial center lifts to the same
physical mark is needed: the balanced circuit supplies the exact
upper bound for EVERY projected candidate.

## 4. Why complete active normals always contain a balanced circuit

At an ordinary deepest point y_* the minimizing unit normals form a
nonempty compact set A. We have

    0 in conv A.                                          (10)

Here is a direct primary-depth proof, avoiding any secondary-objective
constraint qualification. If (10) fails, strict separation gives a
vector v and c>0 with u.v>=c for every u in A. In a neighborhood of
A one has u.v>=c/2. Since y_* lies in int K, moving the center to
y_*-epsilon v increases every such cap by at least C epsilon for
small epsilon, using a fixed ball inside K about y_*. On the compact
complement of this neighborhood the old cap masses exceed A(K) by
a common positive gap. Uniform continuity (or the bounded-section
slab estimate) preserves that gap for small epsilon. All through-point
caps at the moved center would therefore have mass greater than A(K),
contradicting maximality. This proves (10).

If all active normals span U of rank r, Caratheodory in U selects a
balanced family with at most r+1 normals. Delete zero coefficients.
Its own span may have rank s<=r. Section 3 gives D(K)>=Gamma_s>=Gamma_r.
In particular even ONE balanced critical circuit of deficient rank
already gives the corresponding sharper lower bound.

If r=1 in such a family, positive balance forces both antipodal
orientations. Their critical caps partition K up to a null plane, so
D(K)=1/2. Every other pair of opposite through-point caps has total
mass |K| and each has mass at least |K|/2; hence every direction is
active. Therefore the COMPLETE active span is R^d. No ordinary body
in d>1 has complete active span exactly one.

## 5. Sharpness with genuine bodies and the complete active menu

Fix 2<=r<d and put q=d-r>=1. Let T_r be the centered r-simplex

    T_r=conv{(-1,...,-1),(-1,...,-1)+(r+1)e_i:1<=i<=r}.

Let p_T be its Minkowski gauge and form the ordinary d-dimensional
convex body

    K={ (x,w) in R^r x R^q : p_T(x)+|w|<=1 }.             (11)

Equivalently, for |w|<=1 its x-section is (1-|w|)T_r.
Its centroid is zero: every x-section has centroid zero, and the
w-sections are paired by w -> -w. Its volume is

    |K|=omega_q [q! r!/(q+r)!] |T_r|.                     (12)

The canonical horizontal normals are

    (e_i,0), 1<=i<=r,        (-sum_i e_i,0).               (13)

They have a strictly positive balance, span precisely R^r x {0},
and each through-zero cap has fraction Gamma_r by slicing. They
therefore bound the actual maximum depth from above by Gamma_r.

For completeness, the matching all-normal lower bound and the COMPLETE
active menu follow from the archived ordinary paired-tail theorem. For
u!=0 write

    F_u(s)=|T_r intersect {x:u.x>=s}|/|T_r|.

It gives F_u(s)+F_u(-s)>=2 Gamma_r for every s. Pair the sections w
and -w in a through-zero cap with normal (u,v). Their thresholds in
T_r are opposite, namely +/-v.w/(1-|w|). After multiplying by the
common positive section volume and integrating, this proves cap
fraction at least Gamma_r. A purely vertical normal has fraction
1/2>Gamma_r.

If u is not a canonical oriented simplex normal, ordinary simplex
Gruenbaum equality gives F_u(0)>Gamma_r. Continuity preserves a strict
paired excess for all sufficiently small |w|, on a positive-volume set;
the other pairs have nonnegative excess. Thus the full cap is strict.
If u is canonical and v!=0, normalize u so that its simplex vertex
values are r,-1,...,-1. For sufficiently small |s| both cuts are
proper and

    F_u(s)+F_u(-s)
       =[(r-s)^r+(r+s)^r]/(r+1)^r >2 Gamma_r             (14)

whenever s!=0, by strict convexity of t^r for r>=2. The values
s=v.w/(1-|w|) are nonzero on almost every sufficiently small w, so
again the integrated inequality is strict. Consequently ONLY (13),
up to positive scale, are active. Their complete span has rank r,
and the actual ordinary maximum equals Gamma_r. This proves sharpness
for every allowed pair (d,r), not merely for one arbitrary centroid.
The ordinary deepest point is unique by the archived elementary
section-centroid argument; uniqueness is not required for the bound.

The projected density of (11) onto R^r is itself explicit:

    f(x)=omega_q (1-p_T(x))^q 1_T(x).                    (15)

It has the actual positive-power concavity exponent 1/q. Its radial
body at zero is a positive homothetic copy of T_r, so equality in the
radial-centering argument is also realized by a genuinely nonconstant
projected density. Products T_r times a symmetric body give a simpler
constant-density calibration; (11) retains nontrivial fiber heights.

## 6. Scope for critical rate menus

The improvement is exact and depends only on the balanced circuit rank:
Gamma_r replaces Gamma_d, with equality examples above. It is a
statement about actual ordinary MAXIMUM depth and an actual balanced
critical family. A set of limiting cap normals that has low rank but
whose marks cease to maximize the relevant projected law need not meet
these hypotheses. Likewise a finite critical menu without positive
balance does not supply the global upper bound in Section 3.

The radial body is chosen about a new point for one projected measure;
there is no claim that these center choices respect anchored lattice
representations across different fibers or that a mixture of geometric
rate cells remains log-concave. Thus the theorem is a concrete ordinary
rank improvement, not a resolution of the remaining mixed cap payment.

The verifier `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_ball_radial_rank_calibrations_independent.py` passes
466 exact rational calibrations of the beta-integral coefficients, simplex
normal balance and strict paired caps, and the scalar median example.
These checks calibrate formulas; the analytic theorem is proved above.
